claim: Remembering the temporal order of a sequence of events is a task easily performed by humans in everyday life.
source: Remembering the temporal order of a sequence of events is a task easily performed by humans in everyday life, but the underlying neuronal mechanisms are unclear.
evidence: This is a general statement about human cognitive abilities that draws from established understanding.

claim: The underlying neuronal mechanisms for remembering temporal order of sequences are unclear.
source: Remembering the temporal order of a sequence of events is a task easily performed by humans in everyday life, but the underlying neuronal mechanisms are unclear.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Human behavior often proceeds on a time scale of seconds.
source: This problem is particularly intriguing as human behavior often proceeds on a time scale of seconds, which is in stark contrast to the much faster millisecond time-scale of neuronal processing in our brains.
evidence: This is a general observation about behavioral timescales.

claim: Neuronal processing in our brains operates on a millisecond time-scale.
source: This problem is particularly intriguing as human behavior often proceeds on a time scale of seconds, which is in stark contrast to the much faster millisecond time-scale of neuronal processing in our brains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuronal processing speeds.

claim: Phase precession enables the compression of slow behavioral sequences down to the fast time scale of the induction of synaptic plasticity.
source: One long-held hypothesis in sequence learning suggests that a particular temporal fine-structure of neuronal activity — termed 'phase precession' — enables the compression of slow behavioral sequences down to the fast time scale of the induction of synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is described as a long-held hypothesis in the field.

claim: For short enough synaptic learning windows, phase precession can improve temporal-order learning tremendously.
source: Using mathematical analysis and computer simulations, we find that — for short enough synaptic learning windows — phase precession can improve temporal-order learning tremendously and that the asymmetric part of the synaptic learning window is essential for temporal-order learning.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on mathematical analysis and simulations.

claim: The asymmetric part of the synaptic learning window is essential for temporal-order learning.
source: Using mathematical analysis and computer simulations, we find that — for short enough synaptic learning windows — phase precession can improve temporal-order learning tremendously and that the asymmetric part of the synaptic learning window is essential for temporal-order learning.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on mathematical analysis and simulations.

claim: There is only little work on the neural mechanisms generating asymmetric memory associations across behavioral time intervals.
source: It is a pivotal quality for animals to be able to store and recall the order of events ('temporal-order learning', Kahana, 1996; Fortin et al., 2002; Lehn et al., 2009; Bellmund et al., 2020) but there is only little work on the neural mechanisms generating asymmetric memory associations across behavioral time intervals (Drew and Abbott, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Hippocampal place cells signal when an animal visits certain locations in the environment.
source: The slower time scale of behavioral events is mirrored, for example, in the time course of firing rates of hippocampal place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971), which signal when an animal visits certain locations ('place fields') in the environment.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971.

claim: The time scale of the induction of synaptic plasticity is typically milliseconds.
source: The faster time scale is given by the temporal properties of the induction of synaptic plasticity (Markram et al., 1997; Bi and Poo, 1998) — and spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) is a common form of synaptic plasticity that depends on the millisecond timing and temporal order of presynaptic and postsynaptic spiking.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Markram et al., 1997 and Bi and Poo, 1998.

claim: STDP is a common form of synaptic plasticity that depends on the millisecond timing and temporal order of presynaptic and postsynaptic spiking.
source: The faster time scale is given by the temporal properties of the induction of synaptic plasticity (Markram et al., 1997; Bi and Poo, 1998) — and spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) is a common form of synaptic plasticity that depends on the millisecond timing and temporal order of presynaptic and postsynaptic spiking.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Markram et al., 1997 and Bi and Poo, 1998.

claim: Phase precession is the successive across-cycle shift of spike phases from late to early with respect to a background oscillation.
source: Such precisely timed neural activity can be generated by phase precession, which is the successive across-cycle shift of spike phases from late to early with respect to a background oscillation (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a definition supported by reference to Figure 1.

claim: Phase precession can be observed in the activity of hippocampal place cells with respect to the theta oscillation as an animal explores an environment.
source: As an animal explores an environment, phase precession can be observed in the activity of hippocampal place cells with respect to the theta oscillation (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Buzsáki, 2002; Qasim et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Buzsáki, 2002; Qasim et al., 2021.

claim: Phase precession is highly significant in single trials.
source: Phase precession is highly significant in single trials (Schmidt et al., 2009; Reifenstein et al., 2012) and occurs even in first traversals of a place field in a novel environment (Cheng and Frank, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmidt et al., 2009 and Reifenstein et al., 2012.

claim: Phase precession occurs even in first traversals of a place field in a novel environment.
source: Phase precession is highly significant in single trials (Schmidt et al., 2009; Reifenstein et al., 2012) and occurs even in first traversals of a place field in a novel environment (Cheng and Frank, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cheng and Frank, 2008.

claim: Phase precession allows for a temporal compression of a sequence of behavioral events from the time scale of seconds down to milliseconds.
source: Interestingly, phase precession allows for a temporal compression of a sequence of behavioral events from the time scale of seconds down to milliseconds (Figure 1; Skaggs et al., 1996; Tsodyks et al., 1996; Cheng and Frank, 2008), which matches the widths of generic STDP learning windows (Abbott and Nelson, 2000; Bi and Poo, 2001; Froemke et al., 2005; Wittenberg and Wang, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Skaggs et al., 1996; Tsodyks et al., 1996; Cheng and Frank, 2008 and reference to Figure 1.

claim: The temporal compression by phase precession matches the widths of generic STDP learning windows.
source: Interestingly, phase precession allows for a temporal compression of a sequence of behavioral events from the time scale of seconds down to milliseconds (Figure 1; Skaggs et al., 1996; Tsodyks et al., 1996; Cheng and Frank, 2008), which matches the widths of generic STDP learning windows (Abbott and Nelson, 2000; Bi and Poo, 2001; Froemke et al., 2005; Wittenberg and Wang, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Abbott and Nelson, 2000; Bi and Poo, 2001; Froemke et al., 2005; Wittenberg and Wang, 2006.

claim: The putative advantage of phase precession for temporal-order learning has not yet been quantified.
source: This putative advantage of phase precession for temporal-order learning, however, has not yet been quantified.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature.

claim: Phase precession can dramatically facilitate temporal-order learning by increasing the synaptic weight change and the signal-to-noise ratio by up to an order of magnitude.
source: Using both analytical methods and numerical simulations, we find that phase precession can dramatically facilitate temporal-order learning by increasing the synaptic weight change and the signal-to-noise ratio by up to an order of magnitude.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on analytical methods and numerical simulations.

claim: The temporal order of two events is encoded in the asymmetry of the efficacies of synapses that connect neurons representing the two events.
source: We assume that the temporal order of two events is encoded in the asymmetry of the efficacies of synapses that connect neurons representing the two events (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a model assumption stated explicitly.

claim: After successful encoding of a sequence, a neuron that was activated earlier in the sequence has a strengthened connection to a neuron that was activated later in the sequence.
source: After the successful encoding of a sequence, a neuron that was activated earlier in the sequence has a strengthened connection to a neuron that was activated later in the sequence, whereas the connection in the reverse direction may be unchanged or is even weakened.
evidence: This is a model prediction based on the assumed mechanism.

claim: The value σ=0.3 s matches experimental findings on place cells.
source: The value σ=0.3 s, which we use in the example of Figure 2, matches experimental findings on place cells (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Geisler et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to O'Keefe and Recce, 1993 and Geisler et al., 2010.

claim: The maximum benefit of phase precession is about the number of theta oscillation cycles in a firing field.
source: we obtain Bmax≈0.82L/Tθ, that is, the maximum benefit of phase precession is about the number of theta oscillation cycles in a firing field.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis in the study.

claim: Phase precession can boost temporal-order learning by about an order of magnitude for typical cases in which learning windows are narrower than a theta oscillation cycle and overlapping firing fields are an order of magnitude wider than a theta oscillation cycle.
source: We thus conclude that phase precession can boost temporal-order learning by about an order of magnitude for typical cases in which learning windows are narrower than a theta oscillation cycle and overlapping firing fields are an order of magnitude wider than a theta oscillation cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mathematical analysis and simulations.

claim: To achieve SNR≳1 for A=10, one needs M≳14 synapses.
source: Therefore, to achieve SNR≳1 for A=10, one needs M≳14 synapses.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis in the study.

claim: For narrow, odd learning windows (τ≪1/ω≪σ), temporal-order learning could benefit tremendously from phase precession as long as firing fields have some overlap.
source: In summary, for narrow, odd learning windows (τ≪1/ω≪σ), temporal-order learning could benefit tremendously from phase precession as long as firing fields have some overlap.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the analysis.

claim: Average weight changes and the SNR are highest for clearly distinct but still overlapping firing fields.
source: Average weight changes and the SNR are highest, however, for clearly distinct but still overlapping firing fields.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis and simulations.

claim: Any even component of the learning window would increase the noise and thus further decrease the SNR.
source: It should be noted that any even component of the learning window would increase the noise and thus further decrease the SNR.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical properties of the learning window.

claim: For large enough τ, the advantage of phase precession vanishes.
source: Taken together, for large enough τ, the advantage of phase precession vanishes.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: For small enough τ, phase precession increases the SNR.
source: For small enough τ, phase precession increases the SNR, which confirms and generalizes the results in Figure 3C.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Theta oscillations without phase precession degrade temporal-order learning.
source: Remarkably, the SNR for 'phase locking' is lower than the one for 'no theta', which means that theta oscillations without phase precession degrade temporal-order learning, even though theta oscillations as such were emphasized to improve the modification of synaptic strength in many other cases (e.g. Buzsáki, 2002; D'Albis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Temporal-order learning would strongly benefit from wide, asymmetric windows.
source: Taken together, we predict that temporal-order learning would strongly benefit from wide, asymmetric windows.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the analysis.

claim: All experimentally observed (predominantly) asymmetric windows are narrow.
source: However, to date, all experimentally observed (predominantly) asymmetric windows are narrow (e.g. Bi and Poo, 2001; Froemke et al., 2005; Wittenberg and Wang, 2006; see Abbott and Nelson, 2000; Bi and Poo, 2001 for reviews).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: For wide learning windows where the width τ obeys τ≫1/ω, phase precession does not affect the weight change.
source: As already indicated in Figure 4, phase precession does not affect the weight change for such wide learning windows where the width τ of the learning window obeys τ≫1/ω
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: For A=10, the SNR for non-overlapping fields with wide learning windows is approximately 2.2, allowing for temporal-order learning with a single synapse.
source: For A=10, we find SNR≈2.2, allowing for temporal-order learning with a single synapse.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis in the study.

claim: Phase precession facilitates the learning of the temporal order of behavioral sequences for asymmetric learning windows that are shorter than a theta cycle.
source: In this report, we show that phase precession facilitates the learning of the temporal order of behavioral sequences for asymmetric learning windows that are shorter than a theta cycle.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Phase precession bridges the vastly different time scales of the slow sequence of behavioral events and the fast STDP rule.
source: We confirm the long-held hypothesis (Skaggs et al., 1996) that phase precession bridges the vastly different time scales of the slow sequence of behavioral events and the fast STDP rule.
evidence: This confirms a hypothesis from the literature using the study's findings.

claim: Synaptic weight changes can be an order of magnitude higher when phase precession organizes the spiking of multiple cells at the theta time scale as compared to phase-locking cells.
source: Synaptic weight changes can be an order of magnitude higher when phase precession organizes the spiking of multiple cells at the theta time scale as compared to phase-locking cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Drew and Abbott, 2006 suggested STDP and persistent activity of neurons as an alternative mechanism to bridge the time scales of behavioral events and the induction of synaptic plasticity.
source: As an alternative mechanism to bridge the time scales of behavioral events and the induction of synaptic plasticity, Drew and Abbott, 2006 suggested STDP and persistent activity of neurons that code for such events.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: Sato and Yamaguchi, 2003 as well as Shen et al., 2007 investigated the memory storage of behavioral sequences using phase precession and STDP in a network model and found that phase precession facilitates sequence learning.
source: Sato and Yamaguchi, 2003 as well as Shen et al., 2007 investigated the memory storage of behavioral sequences using phase precession and STDP in a network model. In computer simulations, they find that phase precession facilitates sequence learning, which is in line with our results.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work that is consistent with the current study.

claim: A single synapse is not sufficient to reliably encode a minimal two-neuron sequence in a single trial because the fluctuations of the weight change are too large.
source: We find that a single synapse is not sufficient to reliably encode a minimal two-neuron sequence in a single trial because the fluctuations of the weight change are too large.
evidence: This is a finding from the stochastic simulations in the study.

claim: For generic hippocampal place fields and typical STDP, about 14 synapses are sufficient to reliably encode temporal order in a single traversal.
source: For generic hippocampal place fields and typical STDP, we predict that about 14 synapses are sufficient to reliably encode temporal order in a single traversal.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the mathematical analysis in the study.

claim: Peak firing rates of place fields are remarkably high (up to 50 spikes/s).
source: Interestingly, peak firing rates of place fields are remarkably high (up to 50 spikes/s; e.g. O'Keefe and Recce, 1993, Huxter et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to O'Keefe and Recce, 1993 and Huxter et al., 2003.

claim: In hippocampal networks, reliable encoding of the temporal order of a sequence is possible with a low number of synapses.
source: Taken together, in hippocampal networks, reliable encoding of the temporal order of a sequence is possible with a low number of synapses, which matches simulation results on memory replay (Chenkov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis that is consistent with prior simulation results.

claim: For all experimentally found STDP time constants, phase precession can improve temporal-order learning.
source: We show that for all experimentally found STDP time constants phase precession can improve temporal-order learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: For learning windows much wider than a theta oscillation cycle, the benefit of phase precession for temporal-order learning is small.
source: However, for learning windows much wider than a theta oscillation cycle, the benefit of phase precession for temporal-order learning is small.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Wide learning windows, where the width can be even on a behavioral time scale of ≈1 s or larger, could enable the association of non-overlapping firing fields.
source: Wide learning windows, where the width can be even on a behavioral time scale of ≈1 s (Bittner et al., 2017) or larger, could, on the other hand, enable the association of non-overlapping firing fields.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the analysis and a citation to Bittner et al., 2017.

claim: STDP windows typically have symmetric and asymmetric components.
source: STDP windows typically have symmetric and asymmetric components (Abbott and Nelson, 2000; Mishra et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Abbott and Nelson, 2000 and Mishra et al., 2016.

claim: Only the asymmetric component of the STDP window supports the learning of temporal order.
source: We find that only the asymmetric component supports the learning of temporal order.
evidence: This is a finding from the mathematical analysis in the study.

claim: The symmetric component of the STDP window strengthens both forward and backward synapses by the same amount and thus contributes to the association of behavioral events independent of their temporal order.
source: In contrast, the symmetric component strengthens both forward and backward synapses by the same amount and thus contributes to the association of behavioral events independent of their temporal order.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical properties of symmetric learning windows.

claim: The learning window reported by Bittner et al., 2017 shows only a mild asymmetry and is thus unfavorable to store the temporal order of behavioral events.
source: For example, the learning window reported by Bittner et al., 2017 shows only a mild asymmetry and is thus unfavorable to store the temporal order of behavioral events.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis and the properties of the learning window from Bittner et al., 2017.

claim: Only long, predominantly asymmetric STDP windows would allow for effective temporal-order learning.
source: Only long, predominantly asymmetric STDP windows would allow for effective temporal-order learning (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The shape of STDP windows is subject to neuromodulation.
source: Generally, the shape of STDP windows is subject to neuromodulation; for example, cholinergic and adrenergic modulation can alter its polarity and symmetry (Hasselmo, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hasselmo, 1999.

claim: Dopamine can change the symmetry of the learning window.
source: Also dopamine can change the symmetry of the learning window (Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: Sequence learning could be modulated by the behavioral state (attention, reward, etc.) of the animal.
source: Therefore, sequence learning could be modulated by the behavioral state (attention, reward, etc.) of the animal.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the neuromodulation of STDP windows.

claim: For STDP windows narrower (≲10 ms) than a theta cycle (≳100 ms), the slope of the cross-correlation function at zero offset controls the change of the weight of the synapse connecting two neurons.
source: For STDP windows narrower (≲10 ms) than a theta cycle (≳100 ms), we argue that the slope of the cross-correlation function at zero offset controls the change of the weight of the synapse connecting two neurons
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis in the study.

claim: Phase precession can substantially increase the slope of the cross-correlation function at zero offset.
source: and we show that phase precession can substantially increase this slope.
evidence: This is a finding from the mathematical analysis in the study.

claim: Features of the cross-correlation at temporal offsets that are larger than the width of the learning window are irrelevant for temporal-order learning.
source: This result predicts that features of the cross-correlation at temporal offsets that are larger than the width of the learning window are irrelevant for temporal-order learning.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the mathematical analysis.

claim: Phase precession is weak if theta oscillations are weak, as for example in bats and humans.
source: It is thus conceivable to boost temporal-order learning even without phase precession, which is weak if theta oscillations are weak, as for example in bats (Ulanovsky and Moss, 2007) and humans (Herweg and Kahana, 2018; Qasim et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ulanovsky and Moss, 2007; Herweg and Kahana, 2018; Qasim et al., 2021.

claim: Synaptic short-term facilitation has been proposed as a mechanism underlying phase precession.
source: Interestingly, synaptic short-term facilitation, which could generate the described fine structure of the cross-correlation, has also been proposed as mechanism underlying phase precession (Leibold et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leibold et al., 2008.

claim: Recurrent synapses are plastic but weak during encoding, such that they have a negligible influence on the postsynaptic firing rate.
source: In our model, we assumed that recurrent synapses (e.g. between neurons representing a sequence) are plastic but weak during encoding, such that they have a negligible influence on the postsynaptic firing rate
evidence: This is a model assumption stated explicitly.

claim: For the 'encoding' of a sequence, the cross-correlation function is dominated by feedforward input, whereas the recurrent inputs are neglected.
source: and that the feedforward input dominates neuronal activity. These assumptions seem justified as Hasselmo, 1999 indicated that excitatory feedback connections may be suppressed during encoding to avoid interference from previously stored information (see also Haam et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a model assumption supported by citations to Hasselmo, 1999 and Haam et al., 2018.

claim: Phase precession is not generated by the local, recurrent network in the model.
source: The assumption of weak recurrent connections implies that these connections do not affect the dynamics. Consequently (and in contrast to Tsodyks et al., 1996), we thus hypothesize that phase precession is not generated by the local, recurrent network (see also, e.g. Chadwick et al., 2016)
evidence: This is a model assumption and hypothesis stated explicitly.

claim: Phase precession is inherited from upstream feedforward inputs or generated locally by a cellular/synaptic mechanism.
source: instead, we assume that phase precession is inherited from upstream feedforward inputs (Chance, 2012; Jaramillo et al., 2014) or generated locally by a cellular/synaptic mechanism (Magee, 2001; Harris et al., 2002; Mehta et al., 2002; Thurley et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a model assumption supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: After temporal-order learning was successful, the resulting asymmetric connections could generate phase precession.
source: After temporal-order learning was successful, the resulting asymmetric connections could indeed also generate phase precession (as demonstrated by the simulations in Tsodyks et al., 1996), and this phase precession could then even be similar to the one that has initially helped to shape synaptic connections.
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior simulation results.

claim: In the hippocampus, theta oscillations are a traveling wave.
source: In the hippocampus, theta oscillations are a traveling wave (Lubenov and Siapas, 2009; Patel et al., 2012) such that there is a positive phase offset of theta oscillations for the wider firing fields in the more ventral parts of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lubenov and Siapas, 2009 and Patel et al., 2012.

claim: The traveling-wave phenomenon could preserve the temporal order in the phase-precession-induced compressed spike timing.
source: This traveling-wave phenomenon could preserve the temporal order in the phase-precession-induced compressed spike timing, as also pointed out earlier (Leibold and Monsalve-Mercado, 2017; Muller et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to Leibold and Monsalve-Mercado, 2017 and Muller et al., 2018.

claim: Triplet STDP models can reproduce a number of experimental findings that pairwise STDP could not, for example the dependence on the repetition frequency of spike pairs.
source: Triplets STDP models can reproduce a number of experimental findings that pairwise STDP could not, for example the dependence on the repetition frequency of spike pairs (Sjöström et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sjöström et al., 2001.

claim: For the parameters obtained from fitting the triplet STDP model to hippocampal data, only mild differences to the pairwise STDP results were found.
source: for the parameters they obtained from fitting the triplet STDP model to hippocampal data, we found only mild differences to our results (see, e.g. Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations in the study.

claim: A sequence imprinted in recurrent synaptic weights can be replayed during rest or sleep.
source: A sequence imprinted in recurrent synaptic weights can be replayed during rest or sleep (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Nádasdy et al., 1999; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Peyrache et al., 2009; Davidson et al., 2009), which was also observed in network-simulation studies (Matheus Gauy et al., 2020; Malerba and Bazhenov, 2019; Gillett et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple experimental and simulation studies.

claim: The model predicts that phase precession enables efficient and robust temporal-order learning.
source: In conclusion, our model predicts that phase precession enables efficient and robust temporal-order learning.
evidence: This is the main prediction of the study.

claim: The authors suggest experiments that modulate the shape of the STDP window or selectively manipulate phase precession and evaluate memory of temporal order to test the hypothesis.
source: To test this hypothesis, we suggest experiments that modulate the shape of the STDP window or selectively manipulate phase precession and evaluate memory of temporal order.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experiments.
